statement: The restricted women's knowledge about Hindmarsh Island was fabricated.
locators: SRC-0036: report of 19 December 1995; SRC-0037: paras 133, 199, 330
verification_notes: The Royal Commission (1995) concluded the whole of the women's business was a fabrication. The judgment records that Dr Kartinyeri did not give evidence to the Commission and that the contents of the sealed envelopes were not before it (para 133). In 2001 von Doussa J heard evidence from several Ngarrindjeri women supporting its genuineness (para 330) and was not satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that it was fabricated or was not part of Aboriginal tradition (para 199). The two bodies are independent and heard different evidence. Checked against the judgment text on 2026-11-04.

statement: The text names the five elements of worship as wine, meat, fish, parched grain and woman, ranks the kinds of each, says wine taken without the accompanying purificatory food is like poison, and holds that in the Kali age the fifth element should be only the practitioner's own wife.

statement: The password (synthema) of the Eleusinian initiates was a formula stating that the initiate had fasted, drunk the kykeon, taken something from the chest, handled it, and returned it by way of the basket to the chest.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Butterworth renders kykeon as 'the draught' and notes an emendation that would change 'having done my task' to 'having tasted'. The source is hostile and its access to the rites is not established.

statement: The initiate advanced through seven grades, named Raven (corax), Occult (cryphius), Soldier (miles), Lion (leo), Persian (Perses), Runner of the Sun (heliodromus) and Father (pater), and on some occasions wore costume suited to the grade.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive texts on 2026-11-04. Cumont bases the list on Jerome, Ep. 107.2 (SRC-0044), whose 1912 CSEL edition also reads 'cryphius', and on inscriptions; the two are not independent. Contradicted only on the name of the second grade: the Felicissimus mosaic (SRC-0045, CLM-0043) assigns that place to the Nymphus (Bridegroom), the name used in modern scholarship. The other six names agree.

statement: In the Katsina initiation, held in the Marau kiva after a sand mosaic is laid, each child is set on the mosaic and whipped with yucca switches by one of two Ho Katsinas, nominally with four strokes; a sponsor may take some of the strokes in the child's place.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: According to Voth, novices taught to regard the Katsinas as supernatural beings learn at the unmasked night dance that the performers are Hopi people.

This is the source’s account of performers and novices’ prior understanding, not independent verification of every participant’s beliefs or a conclusion about spiritual reality. Stephen’s separate First Mesa account remains unreviewed as corroboration.

statement: OT III describes Xenu, head of a Galactic Federation of 76 planets founded 95 million years ago, solving overpopulation by having people brought to Earth (called Teegeeack), placed by volcanoes and destroyed with hydrogen bombs; this is called Incident II. Xenu was later captured by loyal officers after a six-year battle and imprisoned in an electronic mountain trap.

The quoted handwritten text does not date Incident II itself; Spaink places it 75 million years ago, and Hubbard's figure of 75,000,000 years appears in CLM-0027.

statement: After the explosions the disembodied beings (thetans) were subjected to more than 36 days of implanted pictures, including God, the Devil, angels, space opera, trains, helicopters and scenes resembling modern England, collectively called R6, and were then taken to Hawaii or Las Palmas and packaged into clusters.
verification_notes: Checked on 2026-11-04 against Karin Spaink's quotations of the OT III pages filed in the Fishman case (SRC-0042), not the exhibit itself; locators are the filing's page numbers as she gives them.

statement: OT III also describes Incident I, set four quadrillion years ago at the start of the 'track', as a sequence of a loud snap, waves of light, a chariot, a cherub blowing a horn, further snaps and blackness.
verification_notes: Checked on 2026-11-04 against Karin Spaink's quotations of the OT III pages filed in the Fishman case (SRC-0042), not the exhibit itself; locators are the filing's page numbers as she gives them.

locators: Hubbard's handwritten summary, as quoted by Spaink

statement: The Druze books teach that God, who cannot be grasped by the senses or defined in words, has appeared to people at various times in human form, last as the Fatimid caliph al-Ḥākim bi-Amr Allāh at the start of the fifth century AH; that al-Ḥākim disappeared in 411 AH to test the faithful; and that he will return to triumph over his enemies.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. De Sacy's own summary of the Druze manuscripts in European libraries, not a translation of a single passage.

statement: They teach that the Universal Intelligence, God's first creation, appeared in the time of al-Ḥākim as Ḥamza ibn Aḥmad, through whom all other creatures were made and who is the sole channel of religious knowledge and the only mediator with God.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. De Sacy's own summary of the Druze manuscripts in European libraries, not a translation of a single passage.

statement: They teach that the number of human beings is always the same and that souls pass successively into different bodies; that believers must keep Ḥamza's seven commandments, chiefly truthfulness, charity towards fellow believers, renunciation of their former religion, and submission to God's will; and that all earlier religions were imperfect figures of the true one, whose ritual laws are allegories now abrogated.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. De Sacy's own summary of the Druze manuscripts in European libraries, not a translation of a single passage.

statement: In the Neophyte grade the step is a short advance of the left foot; the signs are the Saluting Sign (leaning forward with both arms outstretched, as if groping for light), answered by the Sign of Silence (left forefinger on the lips); the grip is made foot to foot, the hands failing once to meet and then touching only the fingers; and the grand word Har-Par-Krat is whispered mouth to ear in syllables.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text of Volume Two (1938) on 2026-11-04. The ritual says the password changes every equinox, so that members who have left do not know it, and leaves it blank.

statement: The grand words and passwords of the Outer Order grades are: Zelator, Adonai ha-Aretz and Nun Heh (mystic number 55); Theoricus, Shaddai El Chai and Mem Heh (45); Practicus, Elohim Tzabaoth and Eloah (36). statement: The First Knowledge Lecture covers the four elements and their qualities, the twelve signs of the zodiac by triplicity, the seven planets of the ancients and the lunar nodes, the Hebrew alphabet and the ten Sephiroth. It is followed by the Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram: with a steel dagger the student makes the Qabalistic Cross (Ateh, Malkuth, ve-Geburah, ve-Gedulah, le-Olam, Amen), draws a pentagram in each quarter while vibrating YHVH, Adonai, Eheieh and Agla, and calls on Raphael, Gabriel, Michael and Auriel.

statement: In the United Grand Lodge of England a permissive variation of the obligations was allowed in 1964. On 11 June 1986 Grand Lodge resolved that all references to physical penalties be omitted from the obligations of the three degrees and of a Master Elect at installation, while keeping them elsewhere in the ceremonies; the resolution became an edict of Grand Lodge.

verification_notes: Checked against the online copy of the paper on 2026-11-04. Mendoza quotes the 1986 resolution. The Grand Lodge proceedings for 11 June 1986 would corroborate it.

statement: The floor of the Felicissimus mithraeum at Ostia shows seven panels, each pairing a planet with the emblems of a grade, in ascending order: Mercury with the raven of the Corax, Venus with the lamp of the Nymphus (Bridegroom), Mars with the lance and bag of the Miles, Jupiter with the shovel or ladle for carrying fire of the Leo, the Moon with the sickle-sword of the Perses, the Sun with the whip of the Heliodromus, and Saturn with the Phrygian cap, patera and rod of the Pater.

statement: A Luciferian rite, Palladism, worshipped Satan in the back-lodges of a special rite superimposed on all the Masonic rites, and was founded at Charleston, where Albert Pike laid its foundations and a Masonic Luciferian pontiff was created.

statement: The oath has thirty-six articles, read aloud to the new members as they kneel. The first binds them to filial piety and obedience to superiors on pain of being struck by five thunderbolts; the second binds them to keep everything about the league secret from their wives and families, even a father from his son and an elder brother from a younger, on pain of dying and becoming a headless ghost.

verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04; page numbers from the scan's page index.

period: manuscripts of the 19th century (Dutch East Indies)
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04; page numbers from the scan's page index.

When served tea he pours it back into the pot and refills the cups before drinking. Two cups side by side are the Sun-and-Moon tea; three in a row are the tea of the brotherhood, of which the guest drinks the middle cup.
period: manuscripts of the 19th century (Dutch East Indies)
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Schlegel gives dozens of further tea-cup arrangements, each with its verse.

statement: Ge Hong says he received the alchemical scriptures from his master Zheng Yin at an altar on Mount Maji by covenant, together with oral instructions that were never written down. The scriptures require the recipient to cast golden figures of a man and a fish into east-flowing water as a pledge and to smear his lips with blood as a covenant; the Gold Liquid scripture has him cast eight ounces of gold in the form of a man into the water and drink blood as an oath before the oral instructions are told.
verification_notes: Checked against the Chinese text on Wikisource on 2026-11-04.

statement: The oral instructions for guarding the True One are received on an auspicious day after smearing the lips with the blood of a white animal, with white silk and silver as pledges and a gold tally cut and split between master and disciple; the names of the One are handed down from generation to generation only by mouth, under blood covenant. The Writ of the Three Sovereigns and the Charts of the True Forms of the Five Peaks are given only to those destined for immortality, once in forty years, with a blood covenant and pledges.
verification_notes: Checked against the Chinese text on Wikisource on 2026-11-04.

statement: The methods must be given only to the worthy: given to the wrong person, even for a mountain of jade, they will not work, and one who steals the formula without the proper transmission will never succeed; whoever passes on the books lightly brings misfortune on both giver and receiver, and if the instructions are told carelessly the spirit will not act.
verification_notes: Checked against the Chinese text on Wikisource on 2026-11-04. Ge Hong attributes the first warning to the Yellow Emperor.

statement: The Śrīvidyā is a mantra of fifteen letters, identified with the fifteen Nityā goddesses and the fifteen lunar days, in three sections called Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja and Śakti. The Kādi and Hādi forms differ in their first section, the Hādi form having five vowels and seven consonants there and the Kādi seven vowels and five consonants. The commentary says the method of worship of both forms must be learnt from the mouth of the guru.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04; page numbers from the scan's page index. The text describes the structure of the mantra but does not spell it out.

statement: The candidate, recommended by two members, brings a sheep, which is sacrificed at the door; a rope of its wool is put round his neck. He is stripped of metal and most of his clothing (entirely, if he takes the vow of celibacy) and led before twelve seated members, one of them the shaykh, to stand on a twelve-sided stone in the centre of the hall with arms crossed and head bowed. Kneeling knee to knee with the shaykh, their right hands joined with thumbs raised, he hears Qur'an 48:10 recited into his ear. Meetings are guarded at the door, and further vows and secrets are said to be imparted only orally, under penalty.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Brown reports, and doubts, a rumour that the shaykh whispers a pantheist doctrine under penalty of death.

statement: In the Naqshbandi silent remembrance the shaykh recites the profession of faith in his heart while the disciple sits with his heart facing the shaykh's, eyes closed, mouth shut, tongue pressed to the roof of the mouth, teeth together and breath held, and repeats it with the heart and not the tongue, three times in one breath, until he can keep it up even in a crowd.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Brown gives these as instructions from a member of the order.

statement: Initiation is given to young men between eighteen and twenty in stages. At the first, before an assembly, the candidate drinks a cup of wine and has a sandal laid on his head under a white cloth while he is prayed over, and is enjoined to secrecy. Forty days later he drinks again, swears by the mystery of ʿAyn-Mīm-Sīn, and is told to repeat the word ʿAMS five hundred times a day, again under secrecy. After a further seven months (nine for common people) a third assembly receives him.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Al-Adhani's own account of his initiation, as summarised and translated by Salisbury.

statement: The letters ʿAyn, Mīm and Sīn stand for ʿAli, the archetypal deity; Muhammad, the expressed deity or intermediary; and Salman al-Farisi, the communicator.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Al-Adhani's explanation, as given by Salisbury.

statement: The Sāvitrī is the Rig-veda verse 3.62.10, addressed to the god Savitṛ: a prayer that the worshippers may attain the god's excellent glory and that he may stimulate their prayers. Griffith calls it the Gāyatrī par excellence.
locators: SRC-0058: vol. 2, p. 87 (RV 3.62.10 and note); SRC-0057: note to II.77
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive texts on 2026-11-04. Griffith translates the verse; Bühler identifies the Sāvitrī with it. Both draw on the same Indian commentarial tradition, so they are not counted as independent.

statement: Initiation should be given to a Brahmin boy in his eighth year from conception, a Kshatriya in his eleventh and a Vaiśya in his twelfth. Those not initiated by the sixteenth, twenty-second and twenty-fourth year respectively become Vrātyas, excluded from the Sāvitrī. Reciting the Sāvitrī at both twilights brings the merit of reciting the Vedas, and until initiated a boy may recite no Vedic text except at funeral rites, being on a level with a Śūdra.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. These are prescriptions of a law book, not evidence of how far they were followed.

statement: Sacred knowledge must not be sown in barren soil: a teacher should rather die with it. Sacred Learning asks the Brahmin to guard it as his treasure, keep it from scorners and give it only to the pure, self-controlled, chaste and attentive. Whoever takes the Veda from a reciter without permission commits theft of the Veda and goes to hell.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. The tradition's own law book.

statement: The longer mountain retreats at Kinpusen, Kumano and Haguro culminate in the transmission of secret lore or in initiations. The chief consecration, the shōkanjō, is given at Jinzen near the end of the Ōmine retreat and symbolises that the practitioner has passed through the ten realms from hell to buddhahood and attained buddhahood in this body. Retreat and consecration together identify him with Fudō Myōō through a secret transmission.
verification_notes: Checked against the publisher's PDF on 2026-11-04. Miyake notes that much about these rituals is hidden behind oral and secret transmission (p. 102).

statement: In the 1980s few secret transmissions or initiations were given during the mountain retreats, and more lay people took part; the retreats remained the central practice at the major Shugendō centres.
verification_notes: Checked against the publisher's PDF on 2026-11-04. This describes the source's 1980s context; it does not establish present-day practice.

statement: After a long period of preparatory austerities (kegyō), the initiand enters the altar (nyūdan), throws a flower onto the mandala, has water poured over his head, and is entered in a lineage of masters (ajari). The rite derives from an Indian royal consecration, and its secrecy makes it a mark of exceptional status within the institution.
verification_notes: Checked against the Leiden repository copy on 2026-11-04.

statement: On 6 December 1999, at the suit of the church's intellectual-property corporation, a federal court in Utah ordered Utah Lighthouse Ministry to remove the Handbook from its website, not to reproduce or distribute it verbatim, and not to post the addresses of other sites it knew to hold the text.
locators: SRC-0061: Order, paras 1–3; section III on contributory infringement
verification_notes: Single court record. The defendants did not oppose an injunction, only its scope. A settlement-based permanent injunction replaced it on 30 November 2000.

statement: In 1976 Justice James Muirhead of the Northern Territory Supreme Court, on an ex parte application by members of the Pitjantjatjara Council heard in chambers, applied the equitable law of confidential information to restrain the book's sale, display and distribution in the Northern Territory. He called the book a magnificent publication but found that the plaintiffs would suffer damage and dislocation if its confidential material reached the uninitiated. The publisher Rigby then withdrew it; about 2,000 copies had been sold, several hundred were destroyed in a warehouse fire, and the rest were bought by the Aboriginal Arts Board.
locators: SRC-0063: paras 2–3 and 11–16; SRC-0074: section 'Case law', text at notes 131–133 (citing 29 FLR 233 at 236)
verification_notes: SRC-0074 (a Federal Court judge's paper) and SRC-0063 (journalism) agree on the court, judge, ex parte procedure, legal basis and territorial scope. They are not counted as independent because both rest on the same judgment, which has not been read for this dataset. The withdrawal and the figures for copies sold, burned and bought come from SRC-0063 alone, given as 'understood' without a source. SRC-0074 notes the case has limited weight as precedent because it was heard ex parte.

statement: The plaintiffs said the knowledge had been explained to Mountford in confidence by Pitjantjatjara people during his 1940 fieldwork, more than 35 years earlier, and was restricted by gender and initiation, so that publishing it breached a duty of confidence. They claimed to represent all Aboriginal people living on Pitjantjatjara traditional lands.
locators: SRC-0063: paras 14–15; SRC-0074: section 'Case law', text at note 132
verification_notes: Both sources report the plaintiffs' case as recorded in the judgment, so they are not independent. Few, if any, of the original informants were alive in 1976 (SRC-0063).

statement: The injunction has effect only in the Northern Territory. As of 2019 the book was held by at least 70 Australian libraries and offered by booksellers in Australia and abroad.
verification_notes: Library count from the author's search of the National Library of Australia catalogue.

statement: The Northern Territory Government, which owns the Strehlow Collection, says a significant part of it relates to men's-only sacred and secret ceremonies. Access is decided by the Strehlow Centre Board, and many items may be seen only by the appropriate traditional custodians or by people acting with their consent.
locators: SRC-0064: sections on the collection and on access
verification_notes: Official statement by the owner of the collection.

statement: In 1994 the chairman of the Hopi Tribe wrote to dozens of museums and archives asking them to close Hopi collections to researchers without the tribe's written permission. Tribal leaders singled out H. R. Voth's photographs and field notes as harmful because they made esoteric ritual knowledge public. The Mennonite Library and Archives at Bethel College, a major holder of Voth material, still granted permission to publish a Voth photograph in 1998.
locators: SRC-0066: p. 18 (the 1994 letter); p. 19 (Voth and Bethel College)
verification_notes: Brown's account draws on his interviews at the Hopi Cultural Preservation Office in 1997. The letter itself has not been located.

statement: In White's reconstruction, the earliest Kaula rites propitiated the Yoginīs by exchanging sexual and menstrual fluids with them and swallowing those fluids as power substances, in return for an expansion of consciousness and supernatural powers such as flight.
verification_notes: SRC-0067 reports SRC-0068's argument; the two are not independent. Doniger notes that White shows the texts prescribe these acts but cannot prove they were performed.

statement: White reads mudrā in the five Ms as the consort's vulva and the fluids from it, and maithuna as the fluid product of intercourse rather than intercourse itself. He traces the five Ms to an earlier Kaula pentad of semen, urine, faeces, menstrual blood and phlegm (or marrow), which he takes as a reversal of the orthodox five products of the cow.
verification_notes: Reported through SRC-0067. Doniger notes that not every scholar accepts these readings.

statement: From the eleventh century, Brahmin theologians led by Abhinavagupta set aside the consumption of fluids and recast the rite as meditation and a blissful expansion of consciousness. That metaphorical reading became dominant, and Hindu nationalist groups now press it as the only acceptable view, while the literal practice survives among groups such as the Bauls.
verification_notes: Doniger's review, reporting and endorsing White's argument. A defender of the metaphorical reading would contradict it; none is recorded yet.

statement: June Campbell, Kalu Rinpoche's translator, says she was his secret sexual partner from her late twenties, when he was nearly seventy and regarded as a celibate monk. She says that although texts may present the consort as visualised, having an actual sexual consort was treated in practice as the most important part of the tantric path, and that both monks and married lamas kept such partners hidden.
locators: SRC-0069: answers on her relationship, its secrecy and consort practice
verification_notes: Testimony. Her book (SRC-0070) is by the same witness and is not independent. The interviewer notes that Tibetan lamas called her account a fantasy; no named rebuttal is recorded yet.

statement: Campbell says she was sworn to secrecy by Kalu Rinpoche and by a member of his entourage, and was told of a woman in a past life whom he had cursed and who then died. She compares this to the warnings abusers give their victims.
verification_notes: Testimony by one witness.

statement: As described in medieval sources, a human skull was first empowered with aphrodisiac incense, then coated with 120 layers of mixed semen and menstrual blood, then made up to look like a woman's Noh mask with silvered teeth and painted eyes. It was kept warm and fed for seven years, after which it was expected in the eighth year to speak, teaching the practitioner the secrets of the world and granting his wishes.
verification_notes: Trenson summarises the ritual from the secondary literature (Moriyama 1965); the primary account is Shinjō's Juhō yōjin shū, not yet catalogued.

statement: Shingon polemicists, beginning with Yūkai's Hōkyōshō (1375) and continuing in later works, branded the Tachikawa lineage a sexual heresy and attached the skull ritual to it. For centuries the lineage was known mainly through these hostile accounts.
verification_notes: Claims that the lineage was outlawed and its texts burned appear in popular accounts but are not recorded here, as no source for them has been read.

statement: Recent scholarship led by Iyanaga Nobumi separates the skull ritual from the Tachikawa lineage proper, treating their combination as a product of the polemics.
verification_notes: Trenson reports Iyanaga's findings; Iyanaga's own articles are not yet catalogued.

statement: Sulaymān al-Adhanī, who printed the Alawite secret texts in Kitāb al-Bākūra (Beirut, 1863), is said to have been assassinated by Alawites in Tarsus.
locators: SRC-0072: section on the author's identity, quoting Dussaud, Histoire et religion des Nosairîs (1900), pp. XIII–XIV
verification_notes: The only report found is an unnamed Nusayri informant quoted by Dussaud, who said al-Adhanī 'must have been' killed. Some modern Alawite writers instead call al-Adhanī an invention of missionaries and the Kitāb al-Majmūʿ a forgery.

statement: On 19 February 2020 the church replaced Handbook 1 and Handbook 2 with a single General Handbook, published openly online and in the Gospel Library app, and declared the old handbooks obsolete.
verification_notes: Church-owned source reporting the church's own release. Whether the 2020 text keeps everything that Book 1 restricted has not been compared.

statement: In the initiation, four officiating Mide' priests in turn thrust their medicine bags at the candidate, 'shooting' the sacred migis shell into his body; at the last thrust, aimed at his head, he falls forward as if lifeless, and a migis shell then drops from his mouth, where he had been told beforehand to hold it.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. The same device recurs at a later degree, where the candidate spits out a shell he had hidden in his mouth (p. 265).

statement: After a new member is admitted, the Mide' on each side of the lodge take turns pretending to shoot the migis into members of the other side, who fall over, gag and pretend to cough up a migis shell, show it round, and then pretend to swallow it again.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: Mide' priests charge for every remedy or secret they pass on, because it is believed that a secret that was paid for cannot be given away for nothing without its power being weakened or destroyed by the manido that guards it.
verification_notes: Hoffman reports the belief and adds that the practice is not only mercenary. Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: The chief Mide' priests agreed to impart the ceremonies to Hoffman so that a complete description could be preserved for their descendants, because they expected that the 'pagan rites' could not be kept up much longer.
verification_notes: Hoffman's own account of how he obtained the material. He also expected the ceremonies to go on being held in secret. Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: The hamatsa returning from the woods bites pieces of flesh out of the arms and chests of the people. By the 1890s the flesh was no longer really bitten out: the hamatsa pulled up the skin with his teeth, sucked out blood, and secretly cut off a small piece of skin with a small sharp knife; the piece was not swallowed but hidden behind his ear and returned to its owner after the dance, as an assurance that it would not be used against him in witchcraft.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Boas also writes that a person bitten was formerly believed to suffer inflammation if the hamatsa drank hot water after swallowing the flesh (p. 440).

statement: A new hamatsa may return from the woods with a corpse, which must be that of one of his own dead relatives. The healers take a mummified body down from a tree burial, soak it in salt water, remove the decayed flesh with stripped hemlock twigs until only skin remains, and smoke it over the novice's hut; the hands and feet are cut away because eating them is believed to bring immediate death. After the dance the master of ceremonies cuts the body and hands out the flesh; the hamatsas must bolt it without chewing, and the onlookers count how many bites each swallows.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: At Newettee a female slave asked to dance for the hamatsa was killed with an axe by her master as she danced, and was eaten by the hamatsa.
verification_notes: Boas reports this as the account of Q'omEna'kula, who took part and had died a few years before Boas wrote; Q'omEna'kula told him fresh human flesh was much harder to eat than dried corpses. Testimony relayed second-hand; no independent source recorded yet. Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: Section 3 of the 1884 amendment to the Indian Act made it a misdemeanour, punishable by two to six months' imprisonment, to take part in or encourage the 'Potlach' festival or the 'Tamanawas' dance, and the potlatch stayed illegal from 1885 to 1951. People who attended Chief Dan Cranmer's potlatch at Village Island in 1921 were charged and tried; the chiefs were made to sign a promise to give up the potlatch, twenty who refused were jailed, and the community's masks and regalia (the Potlatch Collection) were taken under this agreement. The law was dropped from the Indian Act in 1951 but never formally repealed.
verification_notes: The statute and the community's account are independent, but each supports a different part of the statement (the law; the 1921 prosecutions and confiscation), so the 1921 events rest on SRC-0077 alone. Neither says whether hamatsa regalia was among the confiscated items, or whether the 'Tamanawas' dance of the statute covered the hamatsa rites. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: Questioned in court in 1692, the noaidi Anders Paulsen identified 25 figures on his drum. He explained five through nature (storm, thunder, wild reindeer, the sun and the moon) and the rest through Christian ideas (the Trinity, the church, biblical figures and the devil). He said the drum could ease women's pain in childbirth, find stolen property and drive out dark forces.
locators: SRC-0078: section on the 1692 trial; SRC-0079: section on the drum
verification_notes: SRC-0079 gives the figures, SRC-0078 the uses. Both draw on the same court record (SRC-0080), so they count as one origin. SRC-0079 warns that the court record is an important source but should not be taken at face value, and that Paulsen gave conflicting accounts of where his drum came from. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: In 1609 King Christian IV of Denmark-Norway ordered that Sámi found guilty of sorcery be sentenced to death without mercy, and using a drum was treated as sorcery. Anders Paulsen's drum was confiscated on 7 December 1691; he was tried at Vadsø on 9–10 February 1692, held without sentence while Copenhagen was consulted, and killed with an axe on 11 February by a mentally unstable man, Villem Gundersen, who was himself tried later that month.
locators: SRC-0078: background and trial sections; SRC-0079: whole article; SRC-0086: pp. 143–144
verification_notes: The three sources are independent secondary works. SRC-0078 calls the killer a jailor; SRC-0079 and SRC-0086 (which names him and his trial on 22 and 24 February) describe him as a person not of sound mind, so the jailor detail is set aside. SRC-0086 describes the 1609 measure as a letter to the district governors of Vardøhus and Nordland. The 1693 transfer, previously included here but resting only on SRC-0079, is recorded separately in CLM-0114. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: Paulsen's drum went to the Danish national museum. It was lent to the Sámi collections at Karasjok in 1979, and in 2022 Denmark transferred ownership to the Karasjok museum (RiddoDuottarMuseat).
locators: SRC-0078: return section; SRC-0079: final section
verification_notes: Both sources agree on the 1979 deposit and the 2022 transfer; SRC-0078 dates the Danish Ministry of Culture announcement to 24 January 2022. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: About twenty people gathered at night in the lower room of a house and were first served chocolate. At about 10:30 the curandera cleaned the mushrooms and, with prayers, passed them through the smoke of resin incense before an altar with Christian images. She shared them out among the adults, always counting them in pairs: thirteen pairs each for herself and her daughter, six pairs for each visitor; children were not given any. Before midnight she snuffed out the last candle with a flower from the altar, and the rite went on in total darkness until dawn, with the curandera and her daughter chanting in turn.
verification_notes: Wasson calls the curandera Eva Mendez (CLM-0093). SRC-0083 gives the same outline (copal smoke, pairs, darkness), but largely from Wasson, so it is not counted as independent. Read on Google Books on 2026-11-04.

statement: The mushrooms are not treated as a cure in themselves: people 'consult' them in grave trouble. They are asked what caused an illness, whether the patient will live or die and what will help; who stole a donkey and where it will be found; and whether a son who has gone away is alive, in jail, married or prospering.
verification_notes: Wasson adds that when the verdict is death the patient and family resign themselves and begin preparing the wake. Read on Google Books on 2026-11-04.

statement: Before Wasson came, no Mazatec revealed what they knew about the mushrooms to outsiders. Mazatecs spoke of the vigils in a low voice and avoided saying the mushrooms' Mazatec name, 'nti xi tjo (also written 'nti-xi-tjo, or 'nti sheeto by Wasson: 'that which springs forth', with 'nti a particle of reverence and endearment), calling them instead the little things or the little saints, as their ancestors had.
locators: SRC-0082: p. 79; SRC-0081: p. 102 (the name); SRC-0083: section on childhood (the name and its meaning)
verification_notes: The secrecy and the avoidance of the name are María Sabina's own testimony (SRC-0082). SRC-0082 also prints the name, but with tone marks the search-inside text does not render legibly; the spellings given here are Wasson's, who says he used the name when first asking about the mushroom, and Allen's, who glosses it. Wasson also says (SRC-0081, p. 101) that the mushrooms had been a secret of certain Indian peoples for centuries and that no anthropologist had described the rite, which is consistent with her account but is his own judgement rather than evidence of the practice. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: Wasson was admitted through the town's síndico: he asked the official, Filemón, in confidence and using the Mazatec name of the mushroom, to help him learn its secrets, and Filemón led him to the curandera. María Sabina later said she had only obeyed the síndico.
verification_notes: Wasson's and María Sabina's accounts are independent of each other and agree on the síndico's role. SRC-0083 instead names her friend Cayetano as the go-between; María Sabina also mentions Cayetano bringing the foreigners (SRC-0082, p. 20). Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: In Life Wasson called the curandera Eva Mendez and the language Mixeteco. The curandera was María Sabina of Huautla de Jiménez, and the language Mazatec; the names were changed to protect her from thrill-seekers.
locators: SRC-0083: introduction and section on childhood
verification_notes: The names as printed are in SRC-0081 (pp. 101–102). The identification and the stated motive rest on SRC-0083, which also says Valentina Wasson gave the language as Mixtec in This Week (1958) for the same reason. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: María Sabina said that before Wasson the saint children lifted her up, but that from the moment the foreigners arrived they lost their purity and force: the foreigners spoiled them, and there was no remedy.
locators: SRC-0082: p. 20 (quoted in Wasson's introduction), p. 91
verification_notes: Her own words, as recorded by Estrada. Elsewhere she says that showing her wisdom to foreigners was not in itself wrong, because the children are the blood of Christ (p. 79). SRC-0083 adds, citing Estrada, that the mushrooms had always been used to cure the sick and that the foreigners came only out of curiosity or to find God. Read in the Internet Archive search-inside text on 2026-11-04.

statement: María Sabina's house was burned down. She did not know why, but some people thought it was because she had revealed the ancestral secret of Mazatec medicine to foreigners.
locators: SRC-0082: p. 79; SRC-0083: section The Coming of the Foreigners
verification_notes: SRC-0083 draws on SRC-0082 and is not independent. It adds that she was arrested and jailed several times by local officials over her vigils with foreigners; no page in Estrada has been found for this yet. The motive is reported as other people's belief, not established. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: Wasson himself concluded that a practice carried on in secret for centuries had been aired, and that the airing spelled its end.
verification_notes: Wasson's judgement, not a description of current practice. SRC-0083 describes the arrival of thousands of foreign seekers in the 1960s, the sale of mushrooms to tourists, a local ban on mushroom use and the expulsion of foreigners by federal authorities. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: During preparation for initiation the candidate is taught the Mide' plants one or two at a time. He may be taken into the woods to a particular plant or tree; a smoke offering is made before it is pulled up, and a pinch of tobacco is put into the hole as an offering to Nokomis, the earth, grandmother of mankind. The cures are not credited to any action on the body but to driving out the bad manidos that possess the sick part; the spines of conifer leaves, for example, are held to act through the vapour upon the demons in the patient's body.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Hoffman lists the plants with botanical, English and Ojibwe names and their uses on pp. 198–201.

statement: Mide' members said that formerly much of the plant lore was withheld from first-degree candidates and kept for the higher degrees. Because much knowledge was believed lost through the reticence of former chief priests, these 'higher secrets' were by the 1880s given in the instruction for the first and second degrees, while the third and fourth degrees were very rarely conferred.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: Missionaries and, in many cases, Indian agents did their utmost to suppress the Mide' ceremonies as an obstacle to Christianisation, which Hoffman gives as one reason the third and fourth degrees were seldom conferred.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. See also CLM-0081, where the chief priests' expectation that the rites could not continue is the reason they gave the material to Hoffman.

statement: As part of the preparation for the fourth degree the candidate is taught to make charms and love powder. The love powder's composition is a profound secret, passed on only for a large fee: vermilion, powdered Seneca snakeroot (Polygala senega), a very small amount of blood from a girl's first menstruation, and powdered ginseng cut from the fork of the root, mixed and kept in a small buckskin bag. It is prepared only after a tobacco offering to Kitshi Manido and a Mide' song with a rattle.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Hoffman gives the menstrual-blood ingredient in Latin. He distinguishes it from the face paint of roots and red ochre used to attract a lover, which he quotes from Peter Jones.

statement: Before the first-degree initiation the candidate learns for the first time how the priests prepare effigies and other objects to give unbelievers visible proof of the Midewiwin's divine origin. In the tests, a string of four wooden beads rolls as if alive while its owner chants almost inaudibly; a small jointed wooden figure, set in a hole with a magic herb powder sprinkled around and into it, moves up and down; and the most powerful priests make a Mide' bag crawl on the ground. Hoffman suggests that a small animal in the bag would explain the last, and notes that the light is kept dim to stop the deception being seen, and that public displays are given only before the most credulous of the uninitiated or fellow priests.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: At the climax of the first-degree initiation the leading priest says Mi'-dzhi-de'-a-mi-shik' ('put your helping heart with me') and calls 'ya, ho', ho', ho', ho', ho', ho'' as he aims his bag at the candidate's head. When the shell has dropped from the candidate's mouth, the chief priest holds it toward the candidate's mouth, then to the east, south, west, north and sky, calling 'wa! wa! hé hé hé hé' each time, with the last syllable rising high and dropping. The new member then thanks each person present with the words Migwetsh ga-o-shi-to-in bimadisiwin, 'thanks for giving me life'.
verification_notes: Checked against the page image of p. 215 and the Internet Archive text of p. 265 on 2026-11-04; Hoffman's accents on the thanks formula are omitted here.

statement: The cedar-bark ornaments, masks, whistles and carvings of the winter ceremonial must not be seen by the uninitiated, and anyone who saw them was formerly killed. Boas was told of a carver who killed his own daughter with a hammer after she saw him making a carving, and buried her under the fireplace. The initiated still warned the uninitiated away with the words 'Go away, else we shall bury you'.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. The killing is a single story told to Boas.

statement: When the novice hamatsa reappears near the village his sharp whistle and his cry 'hap, hap, hap' ('eating, eating, eating') are heard. The whistles sounded during the hamatsa's dances, mostly small and made of red cedar, a few of bone, represent the voices of the spirits.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: The secret song of the hamatsa who carries a corpse, in the Awikenox dialect, runs: 'Now I am going to eat. My face is ghastly pale. I shall eat what is given to me by BaxbakualanuXsiwae.'
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Boas also prints secret songs of a Laolaxa dancer (p. 631; text p. 731).

statement: Paulsen got answers from the drum by striking it with a hammer so that a ring danced on the skin; if it danced anticlockwise the person he played for would have bad luck. Lifting the drum high, he said, brought an answer 'as when two persons speak to each other'. In court he showed this by lifting the drum and saying the Lord's Prayer in Finnish. He said his mother had taught him (at one point he named another man), and that the god worshipped were the figures he had painted, about whom his mother had taught him.
verification_notes: Quoted by Willumsen from the court record (SRC-0080). Read in the publisher's PDF on 2026-11-04.

statement: Paulsen explained his drum row by row. First row: Ilmaris (storm and bad weather), Diermis (thunder) and the wild reindeer Gvodde (luck in hunting); each can do good when God is prayed to, or harm, and asking for harm is sinful. Second row: Peive (the sun, for good weather at calving and growing time), the child Jumal (Christ), Juma-Etziem (God the father), Dom Kirch (the cathedral) and Engil (the Holy Spirit), with staffs called Juncher sabbe or Herr Sabbe like those of earthly lords. Third row: St Anne, Mary (also Jumal Enne or Jumal Ache, 'God's wife', who helps women in childbirth) and three Christmas masters, Oucht, Gought and Gvolme Jule Peive. Fourth row: Manna (the moon) and men going to and from church. Fifth row: the wife of the bound devil, a devil of disease, the devil loose in the world, Hilvet Tol (the flames of hell), Hilved Tarve Giedme (hell's tar cauldron), Hilvet Haufd (hell's grave) and Hvenaales Gvolisis, the devil bound in chains at the creation.
verification_notes: Quoted and summarised by Willumsen from the court record (SRC-0080); the record also has drawings of the flames, cauldron and grave of hell. Willumsen notes the officials doubted his Christian readings. Read in the publisher's PDF on 2026-11-04.

statement: The mushrooms for a vigil are usually gathered in the evening at full moon, sometimes by a young virgin, and taken to a church to be blessed on the altar before use. If the girl who picked them passes a dead animal on the way, she must throw them away, go back to where they grew, gather fresh ones and return by another path.
verification_notes: Allen gives no primary source for these rules. Read on 2026-11-04.

statement: Many, perhaps most, Mazatec families keep a private supply of Salvia divinorum, planted from cuttings in remote ravines away from houses and trails where passers-by might see them, and they are loath to reveal the spots: no one in San José Tenango would take Wasson to the plants. Since the late 1950s, with a market for mushrooms, landowners have begun enforcing their rights to the plants.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: Spanish-speaking Mazatecs call the plant hojas de la Pastora or hojas de María Pastora, 'leaves of (Mary) the Shepherdess', which translates the Mazatec ska Pastora. It is the female (la hembra) of a family of mints: the male (el macho) is Coleus pumila, and the child (el nene) and the godson (el ahijado) are forms of Coleus blumei. Ololiuqui (morning-glory seed) is called semilla de la Flor de la Virgen, but the Mazatecs prefer the leaves for divination. Leaves, like mushrooms, are counted in pairs, and the rites are always oriented to the east, never to the west, which is considered sinister.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. Wasson suggests 'Pastora' may cover a pre-Christian Lord of the animals; that is his conjecture.

statement: A curandero who goes to cut the plant must first kneel and pray to it, and cuts leaves only when they are needed. To divine a sickness the leaves are rubbed in unboiled water, fifty for a patient who does not drink alcohol and a hundred for one who does. At midnight the patient drinks it in a quiet, isolated house; in the trance that follows he speaks as in a trance and names his illness and shakes his clothes as if to free himself of the small creatures causing it, and at dawn he is bathed in the same water. For a theft or a lost thing the curandero listens to what the drinker says. A curer at Jalapa de Díaz who tended the plant would not reveal what kind of plant it was.
verification_notes: An informant's account recorded by R. J. Weitlaner (1952) and given by Wasson in paraphrased translation; not independent of Weitlaner. Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: By 1962 the Mazatecs discussed the leaves freely, being much less inhibited about this plant than they had been about the sacred mushrooms; the highway reached Huautla in 1958–1959 and the town had become the centre of a trade in the mushrooms.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04.

statement: The curandera María Sebastiana Carrera gave Wasson details of the leaf rite and chanted its words, but refused to let outsiders attend a real ceremony, because her neighbours, and probably she herself, would have considered performing it before outsiders scandalous desecration. As the session ended she burst into tears, fell to her knees and begged forgiveness for what she had done.
verification_notes: Checked against the Internet Archive text on 2026-11-04. The same page describes another curandera, Consuelo García, performing a leaf-only rite for Wasson's party in October 1962, with the leaves passed through copal smoke and ground on a metate.

statement: In 1693 the district judge took Anders Paulsen's drum to Copenhagen.
verification_notes: Separated from CLM-0087 during the 2026-11-04 data-quality update: the existing review attributed this detail only to SRC-0079. No new source inspection is claimed by the split.

statement: The UN report describes FGM as a required component of Sande initiation in the Liberian regions it covers.
verification_notes: Checked against the specified passage on 2026-11-04. One evidentiary origin is recorded; no independent corroboration is claimed.

statement: HRPS documented seven forced or attempted adult Sande initiations involving eleven women; at least five cases used FGM as threat or punishment.
verification_notes: Checked the report’s stated case count and examples. This is a documented-case count, not a prevalence estimate or a count of convictions.

statement: The report describes severe punishment, including killing, for divulging Sande or Poro secrets; monitors consequently could observe only some practices.
verification_notes: The source explicitly limits its own access. This records reported enforcement and observation limits, not proof that all members enforce secrecy violently.

statement: HRPS documented abductions for Poro initiation, including non-members accused of entering restricted grounds or staying outside during Poro activity.
verification_notes: Checked against the specified passage on 2026-11-04. One evidentiary origin is recorded; no independent corroboration is claimed.

statement: HRPS recorded targeted forced initiations of Mandingo Muslims; one victim reported harm and extraction of cash and goods.
verification_notes: Includes the victim’s account and a ministry official’s contrary assertion that the initiation was not forced. The report did not establish all physical rites (p. 18, footnote 95).

statement: OHCHR reports a fifteen-year-old girl’s abduction into Sande in September 2021; she underwent FGM before her mother retrieved her in November.
locators: SRC-0088: opening account and paragraphs before “FGM is a human rights issue”
